title: Steady State Concentration -- Definition/Introduction
content: Pharmacokinetics describes the mathematical relationship between the administered dose of a drug and its measured concentration at an easily accessible site in the body. Pharmacokinetics, in particular, is the study of how the body processes a drug, encompassing absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination (the acronym ADME). In pharmacokinetics, the steady state is a concept of fundamental importance in pharmacology. It describes a dynamic equilibrium in which drug concentrations remain within therapeutic limits for extended periods, potentially indefinitely. The concentration at which the drug level remains constant is known as the steady-state concentration .

title: Steady State Concentration -- Definition/Introduction
content: The meaning of steady-state, and its clinical value, can only be understood after the necessary acquisition of some concepts of Pharmacokinetics. In clinical pharmacology and pharmacokinetics, the kinetics of absorption and elimination are complex processes, yet they are governed by basic rules that can be schematized and readily applied across different aspects of drug therapy.

title: Steady State Concentration -- Definition/Introduction
content: The half-life (t1/2) is a key concept in pharmacokinetics. Following repeated administration of a drug, a steady-state is reached when the quantity of drug eliminated in a unit of time equals the quantity of the drug that reaches the systemic circulation in a unit of time. Consequently, the half-life is the time required for the plasma concentration of the drug at steady state to decrease by 50%. The half-life can be calculated with the following formula: t 1/2 = 0,693•Vd/CL

title: Steady State Concentration -- Definition/Introduction
content: Where Vd is the volume of distribution at the steady-state, and CL is the clearance. Although approximate, from a clinical perspective, this formula relates t1/2, Vd, elimination (CL), and steady-state, which are basic Pharmacokinetic parameters. The Vd is defined as the theoretical volume necessary to contain the total quantity of drug present in the organism at the same concentration as that present in the plasma. Thus, the so-called single-compartment model (or 1-compartment open model) was designed assuming that the human body is 1 compartment consisting of a single well-stirred compartment with a Vd; this latter parameter can be calculated with the following equation: Vd = Q/[P]

title: Steady State Concentration -- Definition/Introduction
content: Q is the amount of drug present in the body; [P] is the drug's plasma concentration. Of note, unlike other pharmacokinetic parameters (eg, the rates of absorption, biotransformation, and elimination of the drug from the plasma in units of time), Vd is not subjected to first-order kinetics. Indeed, it does not depend on [P] but on the chemical-physical features of the drug. However, because Vd is an apparent volume, it is not a physical space but a hypothetical space if the drug could distribute uniformly in the body. If the drug concentrations are known, Vd can also be calculated by the formula: Vd = D/C0 Where D is the dose and C0 the concentration at time 0.

title: Steady State Concentration -- Definition/Introduction
content: The other variable of the t1/2 is the clearance (CL). It represents the volume of plasma that is cleaned of the drug in the unit of time and is better defined as the relationship between the rate of elimination of the drug and the concentration of the same in the plasma: CL = drug elimination rate/[P]

title: Steady State Concentration -- Definition/Introduction
content: Although the concentrations of pharmacological agents continuously decrease in the body through metabolism and elimination, periodic administration of the drug, known as maintenance dosing, is necessary to maintain therapeutic concentrations by balancing the rate of drug clearance. Initially, a relatively large dose of the drug can be administered to achieve a therapeutic or steady-state concentration more rapidly; this is known as a loading dose and provides a more consistent initial dose to saturate binding sites.

title: Steady State Concentration -- Definition/Introduction
content: Half-life and Vd formulae are also single-dose pharmacokinetic equations. In the case of multiple infusions, the mathematical approach becomes more complicated. The concept of bioavailability is relevant: the fraction of an administered dose of the unmodified drug that reaches the systemic circulation. For a drug given intravenously, the bioavailability is 100%. When the bioavailability of a drug, the Vd, and the body’s CL of a drug are known, the loading dose and maintenance doses after multiple administrations can be calculated by the following multiple-dose (or infusion rate) equations: LD = SSC•Vd/B In the above equation, LD is the loading dose. MD = SSC•CL•DI/B MD is the maintenance dose, SSC is the desired steady-state concentration of the drug, B is the drug's bioavailability, and DI is the dosing interval.

title: Steady State Concentration -- Definition/Introduction
content: A fundamental aspect requiring attention is the evaluation of drug plasma concentrations following multiple administrations, accounting for both non-saturable and saturable mechanisms. In clinical terms, the clinical differences are striking. In particular, if the absorption and elimination systems are not saturable for small dosing increments, the increase in the concentration of the drug is proportionate. In this case, the drugs follow first-order kinetics. According to this model, a constant fraction of the drug is eliminated in a unit of time, and, in turn, the kinetics are exponential. The rate of elimination is directly proportional to drug concentration, which, in turn, decays exponentially.

title: Steady State Concentration -- Definition/Introduction
content: On the other hand, if the absorption and elimination systems are saturable, a zero-order (or saturation) kinetics is followed. In this model, the kinetics are not exponential; they are initially linear because drug removal occurs at a constant rate that is independent of plasma concentration. After saturation, the relationship between the administered dose and the steady-state plasma concentration is unpredictable, not following the rule of proportionality. When the system is saturated, indeed, increases in the administered dose does not correspond to increases in plasma concentrations, and small changes in dose may induce a significant change in plasma concentrations; interestingly, while the absorption of most drugs follows first-order kinetics, several drugs, such as ethanol, phenytoin, and aspiri,n exhibit saturation kinetics, especially at toxic concentrations. Accumulation

title: Steady State Concentration -- Definition/Introduction
content: Drug accumulation occurs with repeated dosing (dosing interval), and there is a delay in the time to eliminate the drug from the body. This phenomenon usually manifests when the dosing interval is shorter than 4 half-lives. An index of accumulation is the accumulation ratio (AR): AR = 1 dose/FD

This formula's first-order kinetics for the drug can predict the AR across various dosing regimens by varying the dosing interval. title: Steady State Concentration -- Issues of Concern
content: A major concern is the half-life. To predict its changes, indeed, it is necessary to know the status of both the main variables that determine it, including Vd and CL. In general, disease, age, and other variables may alter a drug's CL much more than its Vd. On the contrary, in some circumstances, such as in elderly individuals, body fat increases (up to 36% in men and 45% in women), which can induce a longer t1/2 for lipophilic drugs. Furthermore, in this setting of reduced lean body mass, a reduction of total body water with an increase in plasma concentration of hydrophilic drugs, a decrease of serum albumin with an increased free fraction of highly protein-bound acid drugs, and an increase in acid a1-glycoprotein with a decrease of the free fraction in the plasma of basic drugs (eg, tricyclic antidepressants, antipsychotics, beta-blockers), there are pharmacokinetics changes to consider during drug therapy. These variations usually have little clinical relevance, except for drugs with high plasma protein binding, low Vd, and a narrow therapeutic index. [1] Because some drugs, such as opioids, can significantly increase the toxicity profile, the pharmacokinetic modifications must merit consideration, necessitate dosage changes, and adjust the administration intervals. [2] [3]

title: Steady State Concentration -- Issues of Concern
content: Another important factor to consider is the mechanism by which a steady state is achieved and the factors that can modify it. An appropriate loading dose is necessary to achieve therapeutic concentrations more quickly, similar to those achieved at steady state. The steady-state concentration can also be achieved with a series of close-spaced administrations, thereby achieving the plasma concentration required for the therapeutic effect in a very short time. It is then possible to continue maintenance doses. Although a pharmacological rule of thumb states that steady-state concentration is reached in approximately 5 half-lives, there are notable exceptions. Some drugs do not follow conventional 1- or 2-compartment models or exhibit non-exponential decay (eg, ethanol has zero-order elimination); thus, this rule of thumb may not apply to them. [4] Additionally, the liver and kidneys eliminate many known drugs. Hepatic or renal dysfunction can alter the pharmacokinetics of drug elimination, changing a drug’s half-life. [5] Consequently, the time to steady-state concentration can change. Although the drug’s loading dose generally does not need to be changed, if the same steady-state concentration is desired, the drug’s maintenance dose (drug addition) should be adjusted to compensate for the change in elimination (drug removal). [6] [7]

title: Steady State Concentration -- Clinical Significance
content: Reaching a steady-state concentration is generally necessary for effective pharmacological management of diseases. An example is the use of antibiotics to treat infectious diseases. [8] Serum antibiotic concentrations must remain within a clinically effective range for optimal treatment. Concentrations below this range may be insufficient to treat infections, and levels above this range may cause toxicity. [9] Subtherapeutic concentrations correlate with antibiotic resistance. [10] Analogously, most drugs are studied at specific doses that yield desirable steady-state concentrations, with medical therapy dependent on consistent dose adherence to achieve these predetermined concentrations. In other words, therapeutic drug monitoring should take place in a steady state.

title: Steady State Concentration -- Clinical Significance
content: The concept of constant state is crucial in specific clinical settings, such as general anesthesia. In particular, in total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA) and targeted-controlled infusion (TCI) approaches, drug kinetics, such as those of propofol and remifentanil, are used to maintain a constant blood concentration and, therefore, a predictable concentration at the site of action (brain).

title: Steady State Concentration -- Nursing, Allied Health, and Interprofessional Team Interventions
content: All healthcare practitioners at any level need to be familiar with the concepts of drug steady-state concentration. The pharmacist must be the expert in initial loading doses, maintenance dosing, and monitoring of relevant parameters to ensure steady-state drug levels. This can include educating and communicating with other interprofessional healthcare team members regarding steady-state concentration and factors that affect it. This type of interprofessional collaboration leads to better outcomes in patients' pharmaceutical therapy.
